title: Why he left
hook: he left the woods because he had several more lives to live (Walden 18)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last lines of Walden, and your line: more day to dawn. Which part of the day were you awake for? Day one thousand two hundred forty-five.

Why would anyone walk away from the place they wrote a whole book loving? The cabin was built with his own hands. The pond was the one he sounded through the ice. The bean rows, the loon, the ant war, the thaw. And then he packed up and went back to town. Readers still ask it: if the woods were so good, why leave? Thoreau saw the question coming, and in his last chapter he answers it in two sentences. They're plain, and they sound less like an apology than a doorway.
screen: `HE BUILT IT. HE LOVED IT.` → `THEN HE LEFT.` → `TWO SENTENCES OF ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Here they are: "I left the woods for as good a reason as I went there. Perhaps it seemed to me that I had several more lives to live, and could not spare any more time for that one." First, as good a reason as I went there. Back near the start of the book he had said, "I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately." So leaving gets the same respect as going. It wasn't a failure or a retreat. It was the same deliberate choice, pointed the other way. Second, several more lives. Not one life with a long detour at a pond. Several lives, one after another, and Walden was one of them. That's a roomy way to see a single lifetime: chapters that are each whole. Third, the warning that comes right after. Thoreau says it's remarkable how easily and quietly we fall into a route, and "make a beaten track for ourselves." He noticed that before long his own feet had worn a path from his door down to the water. Even in the woods, even in a life chosen on purpose, a groove forms. And a groove can become a rut. Fourth, what his answer leaves out. Nothing in it says the cabin had gone stale or the experiment had failed. He says only that he could not spare any more time for that one life, because there were others waiting. The pond didn't fail him. He just had more lives to get to.
screen: `AS GOOD A REASON AS I WENT.` · `SEVERAL MORE LIVES TO LIVE.` · `A BEATEN TRACK FOR OURSELVES.` · then, large: `NO MORE TIME FOR THAT ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: end one chapter. Settle and breathe. Let one part of your life come to mind that has quietly finished, or is ready to. A habit, a role, a routine, a worry you've walked so often it's worn a path. Don't judge it. Thank it for what it gave you. Then, in your own words, tell it that this chapter is over. Notice the space it leaves. You don't need to know what the next life is. Just let this one close. The bell holds the time.
Why he left. Thoreau's answer: he left the woods for as good a reason as he went, because he had several more lives to live. Today's word.
Your line: several more lives. Today, notice one beaten track you walk without thinking, and take a different way once, just to see. Day one thousand two hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Readers often take Thoreau's reason for leaving Walden as permission to close a good chapter on purpose, before it hardens into habit, and to treat a life as several lives in turn.

notes: Confirm exact wording against the 1854 text: the 'I left the woods' passage, 'I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately', and 'make a beaten track for ourselves'.
Paraphrased: 'It is remarkable how easily and insensibly we fall into a particular route'; and the path to the pond-side, which Thoreau says his feet wore within a week (the number is left out).

Editor pass: removed a repeated 'ice' in the hook and an unsourced superlative ('some of the plainest in the book'); the fourth teach step now stays with what Thoreau's two sentences say instead of inferring he left 'while it was still good'.
